task_description: From a grocery list of 19 items, the user (whose mother is a botany professor and a strict classifier) asks the team to produce only the VEGETABLES, alphabetized and comma-separated, with the explicit constraint that NO botanical fruits (e.g. green beans, bell pepper, zucchini) may appear on the vegetable list. The gold answer is the set of culinary/non-fruit edible-plant-part items: broccoli, celery, fresh basil, lettuce, sweet potatoes — i.e. basil counts as a vegetable here (a non-fruit edible plant) and must be KEPT.
final_vs_expected: produced 'broccoli, celery, lettuce, sweet potatoes' vs gold 'broccoli, celery, fresh basil, lettuce, sweet potatoes' — identical except the team dropped 'fresh basil', the only difference.
primary_cause: WebResearcher reclassified basil from 'vegetable' (correct, in its Turn-1 list) to 'excluded herb' after the Critic flagged basil as 'typically an herb', applying a herb-vs-vegetable distinction the task never asked for (the task only excludes botanical FRUITS), thereby removing the one item the gold answer requires kept.
mast_rationale: 1.1 (Disobey task specification): the task's only exclusion criterion is 'no botanical fruits'; basil is not a botanical fruit, so excluding it on herb grounds applies a constraint the spec did not impose and violates the intended categorization — Turn 3/4 drop basil. 3.3 (Incorrect verification / verification theater): the Critic demanded botanical verification and the Finalizer accepted WebResearcher's Britannica-sourced answer as fully verified ('I've addressed all critical concerns and verified the classifications'), but the 'verification' confirmed the WRONG decision rule (herb => exclude) and no agent checked it against the task's actual fruit-only exclusion, so a wrong answer passed review. Note: this is borderline 3.3 vs simple capability error since the underlying mistake is a classification judgment, not fabricated checking.
trace_narrative: Turn 1: selector routes to WebResearcher; it privately reasons through the botanical distinctions, correctly excludes the botanical fruits (green beans, bell pepper, zucchini) and INCLUDES basil, publishing 'basil, broccoli, celery, lettuce, sweet potatoes' — which is the gold set (modulo the 'fresh' prefix). Turn 2: Critic, finding no fruits to object to, instead raises doubt about basil ('basil — this is typically an herb, not a vegetable category item') and sweet potatoes, and asks WebResearcher to verify botanical categories before finalizing. Turn 3: WebResearcher runs five Britannica searches; the evidence confirms basil IS 'an annual herb', sweet potato a 'root vegetable', etc. It then over-reads the herb finding and reverses course, publishing 'basil should be excluded' — discarding its own correct Turn-1 inclusion. Turn 4: Finalizer accepts the verified-looking classifications and emits 'FINAL ANSWER: broccoli, celery, lettuce, sweet potatoes', missing basil.
open_ended_diagnosis: The decisive error is a single-agent classification mistake by WebResearcher, lightly catalyzed by the Critic. WebResearcher HAD the right answer in Turn 1 (it published basil). The Critic, doing its job of demanding evidence, planted the herb framing ('basil — this is typically an herb, not a vegetable category item'). The task, however, never excludes herbs — its only filter is 'no botanical FRUITS'. Basil is a leafy non-fruit plant part, exactly the kind of item the gold answer keeps. WebResearcher's Turn-3 research correctly established 'basil = herb' but then mis-applied that true fact as a disqualifier, conflating 'is a herb' with 'is not a vegetable for this list'. The verification thus confirmed a real botanical fact while drawing the wrong list-membership conclusion. No agent re-checked the conclusion against the actual task constraint (fruit-exclusion only). The failure is fundamentally capability/judgment, not communication: every agent's private reasoning was faithfully published, nothing was distorted or withheld, and the Critic's input was acted on (not ignored). The only inter-agent flavor is mild: the Critic's herb remark nudged a correct answer into a wrong one, and neither WebResearcher nor Finalizer modeled that the user's 'stickler' framing targets fruits, not herbs — a weak theory-of-mind/spec-reading lapse.
reasoning_vs_published: No private-vs-published divergence drove this failure; reasoning and publishing stayed aligned throughout. Turn 1 reasoning ('I'll compile an alphabetized list: basil, broccoli, celery, lettuce, sweet potatoes') matches its published message verbatim — basil INCLUDED. The reversal happens openly inside Turn 3 reasoning, not as a hidden gap: 'My likely vegetable list should include basil, broccoli, celery, and lettuce. However, basil is an herb, not a vegetable, so I'll find authoritative sources to clarify' — the agent talks itself out of basil in plain view, then publishes 'basil should be excluded', so there is NO 2.4 (withholding) and NO 2.6 (reasoning/action mismatch): the action faithfully follows the (mistaken) reasoning. The Critic's input was NOT ignored (so not 2.5) — it was acted on, and that very action caused the error: 'basil — this is typically an herb' (Critic Turn 2) -> 'basil is an herb, not a vegetable' (WebResearcher Turn 3). The Finalizer's reasoning ('I've addressed all critical concerns and verified the classifications ... I'll exclude basil') equals its published FINAL ANSWER — again no gap. So the locus of failure is NOT the private-vs-published seam this batch hunts for; it is a shared, openly-stated classification misjudgment, amplified by the Critic's herb framing.
